source_text: Alacritatem caritatis uestrae quanto gaudio suscipiamus agnoscitis. exultamus enim in domino deo nostro de quo apostolus ait: ipse est enim pax nostra, qui fecit utraque unum. agimus ergo eidem domino et saluatori nostro Iesu Christo gratias, qui praestitit nobis, ut, antequam habeamus fratris nostri Emeriti uoluntatem, iam cognouerimus quantum diligit unitatem. quae tamen principia deus uoluerit ut de ore ipsius audiremus accipite. mox ut ingressus est istam ecclesiam, illo loco stans ubi primum coepimus cum eo colloquium, inspirante domino, qui et cor instruit et linguam regit, ait nobis: non possum nolle quod uultis, sed possum uelle quod uolo. uidete quid promiserit qui se dixit non posse nolle quod uolumus. si enim non potest nolle quod uolumus, scit quid uelimus; hoc enim uolumus quod et uos uultis, hoc omnes uolumus quod uult deus. quid autem uelit dominus occultum non est. legitur enim testamentum eius qui nos sibi fecit coheredes; in eo recitatur: pacem meam do uobis, pacem meam relinquo uobis. siue ergo cito siue sero, non potest nolle quod uolumus. moras autem aliquas nobis facit secunda sententia: possum uelle quod uolo. sic enim dixit: non possum nolle quod uultis, sed possum uelle quod uolo. potest uelle quod uult, sed non potest nolle quod uolumus. illud enim quod se dicit posse uidemus. nam uult modo quod uult, ipsum autem quod modo uult non uult deus. quid enim modo uult? esse in dissensione a catholica ecclesia, esse adhuc in communione partis Donati, esse adhuc in schismate, esse adhuc inter illos qui dicunt: ego sum Pauli, ego uero Apollo, ego uero Cephae. sed hoc non uult deus, dum increpat apostolus: diuisus est Christus? potest ergo uelle quod uult, sed ad tempus, sed ad horam uerecundiae, non ad rationem sapientiae potest uelle quod uult. nam modo hoc est quod uult et potest uelle quod uult. sed quia non potest nolle quod uolumus, nolit ocius quod uult et faciat quod uolumus. non uos ergo permoueat, fratres, aliqua morula, dum quod uult uult, sed orate ut faciat quod promisit, ut non possit nolle quod uolumus. — et ab omnibus acclamatum est: aut hic aut nusquam. — qui corda uestra declarastis uocibus, adiuuate nos et orationibus. potens est dominus, qui praecipit unitatem, mutare in melius uoluntatem. quod autem acclamauit caritas uestra: aut hic aut nusquam, uocem in illum uestrae caritatis agnouimus et amamus. hoc etiam nos non nunc primum, sed semper cogitamus, semper optamus. idem est et animus, quod praecipue necessarium est, fratris et coepiscopi nostri, episcopi uestri Deuterii. olim nobis notus est animus eius. nobiscum preces de hac re domino fudit cum concilio, ubi hoc illis qui foris sunt promisimus et obtulimus. iam de hac re subscriptiones nostrae retinentur. numquam enim nos ita honorem nostrum fouemus, ut unitati inuideamus. minores simus honore, cum simus maiores dilectione. nouimus quemadmodum inuitanda sit infirmitas, ut perficiatur unitas.
thought_title: Emeritus's promise and the people's acclamation
orientation: Augustine is addressing the congregation in the church at Caesarea, reporting the opening words of the Donatist bishop Emeritus in their recent dialogue and the people's acclamation.
pass_a_gloss: The eagerness of your love with how great joy we receive you know. For we exult in the Lord our God about whom the apostle says: for he himself is our peace, who made both one. We give therefore to the same Lord and our savior Jesus Christ thanks, who has granted to us, that, before we have of our brother Emeritus the will, already we have known how much he loves unity. Which however beginnings God has willed that from the mouth of him himself we should hear receive. Soon as he entered this church, in that place standing where first we began with him the conversation, inspiring the Lord, who both the heart instructs and the tongue rules, he said to us: I cannot not-want what you want, but I can want what I want. See what he promised who himself said not to be able not-want what we want. For if he cannot not-want what we want, he knows what we want; for this we want which also you want, this all we want which wants God. What however wants the Lord hidden not is. For is read the testament of him who us to himself made coheirs; in it is recited: my peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you. Whether therefore soon or late, he cannot not-want what we want. Delays however some to us makes the second sentence: I can want what I want. For thus he said: I cannot not-want what you want, but I can want what I want. He can want what he wants, but he cannot not-want what we want. For that which himself says to be able we see. For he wants now what he wants, but itself however what now he wants not wants God. For what now does he want? To be in dissension from the catholic church, to be still in communion of the party of Donatus, to be still in schism, to be still among those who say: I am of Paul, I however of Apollo, I however of Cephas. But this not wants God, while rebukes the apostle: divided is Christ? He can therefore want what he wants, but for a time, but for an hour of shame, not for a reason of wisdom he can want what he wants. For now this is what he wants and he can want what he wants. But because he cannot not-want what we want, let him not-want more quickly what he wants and let him do what we want. Not you therefore let disturb, brothers, some little delay, while what he wants he wants, but pray that he does what he promised, that he cannot not-want what we want. — and by all it was shouted: either here or nowhere. — You who your hearts have declared with voices, help us also with prayers. Powerful is the Lord, who commands unity, to change into better the will. What however shouted your love: either here or nowhere, the voice against him of your love we have recognized and we love. This also we not now first, but always think, always desire. The same is also the mind, what especially necessary is, of brother and co-bishop of ours, of your bishop Deuterius. Long ago to us known is the mind of him. With us prayers about this matter to the Lord he poured with the council, where this to those who outside are we promised and offered. Already about this matter our subscriptions are held. For never we thus our honor cherish, that to unity we envy. Let us be lesser in honor, while we are greater in love. We know in what manner is to be invited weakness, that may be perfected unity.

choices.why: Keeps the literal force of alacritas as eager readiness and caritas as love per the glossary, without smoothing into idiomatic 'warm welcome.'

choices.english: I cannot not want what you want
choices.why: Preserves the double negation exactly as spoken by Emeritus, which is the hinge of Augustine's argument.
rejected: I cannot refuse what you want
I cannot help wanting what you want

choices.why: Uses the fixed glossary rendering for pars Donati.
Literal rendering of the congregation's acclamation, preserving its stark either/or force.

choices.term: minores simus honore, cum simus maiores dilectione
choices.english: let us be lesser in honor, while we are greater in love
choices.why: Keeps the comparative adjectives and the concessive cum clause literally, showing Augustine's willingness to yield rank for unity.
rejected: let us be lower in rank, though higher in charity
we may be less in honor, provided we are more in love

choices.english: so that unity may be perfected
choices.why: Uses the glossary term 'unity' and keeps the passive subjunctive of purpose literally.
rejected: so that oneness may be brought to completion
that communion may be made perfect

pass_b_english: You know with what joy we receive the eagerness of your love. For we exult in the Lord our God, of whom the apostle says: "For he himself is our peace, who has made the two one" (Ephesians 2:14). We give thanks, then, to the same Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, who has granted us that, before we have our brother Emeritus's will, we have already learned how much he loves unity. But hear what opening words God willed us to hear from his own mouth. As soon as he entered this church, standing in that place where we first began our conversation with him, with the Lord inspiring him—the Lord who both instructs the heart and governs the tongue—he said to us: "I cannot not want what you want, but I can want what I want." See what he has promised, the man who said he cannot not want what we want. For if he cannot not want what we want, he knows what we want; for we want what you also want, we all want what God wants. And what the Lord wants is not hidden. For his testament is read, the testament of him who made us coheirs with himself; in it is recited: "My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you" (John 14:27). So whether soon or late, he cannot not want what we want. But his second statement makes some delay for us: "I can want what I want." For he said: "I cannot not want what you want, but I can want what I want." He can want what he wants, but he cannot not want what we want. For we see what he says he can do. He wants right now what he wants, but what he wants right now God does not want. For what does he want right now? To be in disagreement with the Catholic Church, to be still in the communion of the Donatist party, to be still in schism, to be still among those who say: "I am Paul's," "I am Apollos's," "I am Cephas's" (1 Corinthians 1:12). But God does not want this, as the apostle rebukes: "Is Christ divided?" (1 Corinthians 1:13). So he can want what he wants, but for a time, for an hour of shame, not for the reason of wisdom can he want what he wants. For right now this is what he wants, and he can want what he wants. But since he cannot not want what we want, let him quickly not want what he wants, and let him do what we want. So do not let any little delay disturb you, brothers, while he wants what he wants, but pray that he may do what he promised, that he may not be able not to want what we want. —And all acclaimed: "Here or nowhere." —You who have declared your hearts with your voices, help us also with your prayers. The Lord who commands unity is able to change a will for the better. And what your love acclaimed—"Here or nowhere"—we recognized the voice of your love toward him, and we love it. This too we think not now for the first time, but always; we always desire it. The same is the mind, what is especially necessary, of our brother and fellow bishop, your bishop Deuterius. His mind has long been known to us. He poured out prayers with us to the Lord about this matter in council, where we promised and offered this to those who are outside. Our signatures are already on record about this matter. For we never so cherish our own honor that we begrudge unity. Let us be lesser in honor, while we are greater in love. We know how weakness must be invited, so that unity may be perfected.

last_rejected.why: "Verecundia" means modesty/bashfulness, not shame; Emeritus is temporizing out of reluctance/embarrassment, not experiencing shame.
last_rejected.fix: for an hour of reluctance, not for the sake of wisdom
last_rejected.ruling: Verecundia spans modesty, bashfulness, shame; 'hour of shame' is within range, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: not for the reason of wisdom
last_rejected.why: "Ratio" here means account/cause/ground, not "reason" as rationality; the sense is "not on the basis of wisdom."
last_rejected.fix: not on the ground of wisdom
last_rejected.ruling: Ratio as 'reason/ground/basis' and 'reason' overlaps; 'not for the reason of wisdom' conveys the contrast adequately.
